[b]Battle of Minproki[/b]

MROS Dynamics would finish setting up shaky defensive fortifications along the SLF salient overlooking Minproki. Wooden and concrete pillboxes, if there were any left, would be swiftly cleaned up by ARoS workers and staffed with both MROS contractors and Brigrada XXIV militiamen, while shallow trenches lined the frontlines together with ATGM sites and machine gun nests in preparation for the SLF advance. Whatever reservists that the ARoS could muster up would be also called in and swiftly armed within the day and thrown together with MROS forces to pad their forces for what's to come.

Operations manager David Cyriacus, clearly lacking faith in the reliability of the ARoS's forces, would also direct demolition efforts to destroy any strategic bridges, railways, and tunnels that SLF militants could potentially use to flood into ARoS territories, while on the home front leaflets and "resistance kits" would be distributed by MROS personnel to ARoS civilians, consisting of surplus rifles, ammunition, and simple guides to guerilla tactics based primarily from SummitONE Solutions' training guidebook.

While this was ongoing, MROS Dynamics would begin putting pressure on ARoS forces to begin loading their valuables onto corporate vessels to be evacuated to safety elsewhere in the event of total military defeat on the frontlines.

After both ARoS and SLF explicitly rejected the idea of an externally backed government, Hydronia reached out to the members of THEP with a crucial proposal. They cautioned against the potential risks of establishing a Thýven-backed state in Sikirsk, emphasizing that such an initiative could significantly complicate and destabilize an already fragile situation. 

Instead, Hydronia has recommended that THEP consider funding the SLF. Supporting the SLF could yield outcomes that align closely with THEPs interests. By aiding the SLF in their quest to establish a democratic governmentan essential tenet of THEPs philosophyTHEP could not only foster a more stable political environment in Sikirsk but also cultivate a collaborative relationship with the SLF for future endeavors.

Moreover, backing the SLF would pave the way for a brighter future for the citizens of Sikirsk, allowing them to thrive under a democratic regime rather than one solely focused on arms sales and neglecting the well-being of its people. This strategic move not only serves to advance THEPs values but also ensures that the people of Sikirsk are represented and cared for within a government that prioritizes their interests.

A beautiful morning dawns over Sikirsk, signalling yet another day of fighting for the three opposing governments, and another day of survival for the refugees in the SRZ. As the sun rises, it illuminates the ships on the water. Many are fishing vessels or simply ferries, but a convoy of ships stands above the rest. Adorned in blue paint and large white letters on either side, its apparent these transports arent from any side in the civil war. Onlookers watch as they prepare to enter the harbor, and inside the ship, a guardsman dreams of home.

Through the hum of the ship and the commencement of its morning duties, a song interrupts the white noise in the cabin. A bunch of frightened rookies were listening, filled with awe. They listened while the sergeant was laying down the law! They stood there at attention, their faces turning red! The sergeant looked them over and this is what he said: This is the army mister Jo-. After finding his phone somewhere on the floor, this soldier silences his lyrical alarm and stares at the ceiling. After a few moments, he gets up, gets dressed, and exits his rool to head up to the deck. Greeting a few of his friends on the way, he finally leans against the railing, peering out at the small figures on the shore. He figures some of them are completing their morning errands, buying food, or are just simply going to work, but that's a given after all. Taking a sip of coffee that he acquired from a friend in the mess hall, he takes a few moments to ponder why hes here. To protect people? Obviously, but why him? So many to pick from and yet he was sent. Was it based on last names? Birth dates? Who knows. He takes a while to finish his coffee, then finally heads down to the cargo area to help prepare everything for unloading.

	Hours later, treads of blue APCs and IFVs rumble along Sikirsk streets, heading to the border of the city. Behind them, trucks loaded with food and aid for the people of the SRZ follow, creating a sizable perimeter. In buildings near the port, vacant shop fronts are turned into aid stations, makeshift hospitals, and shelters for those who have lost homes. Our soldier finds himself assigned to stacking sandbags at an entrance checkpoint being set up. He knows this most likely wont go over well with everyone, but a few irate people is better than a massacre and looting of a city. He mindlessly stacks sandbags while he watches the APC assigned to this checkpoint go through general servicing by its crew. Everyone is preparing for something to happen, but its unlikely. This far into the refugee zone, nobody but refugees travel this far. The few ARoS stragglers near the border of the zone are too busy terrorizing small towns, and most definitely dont have the strength to raid this far in and this size of a city under protection right?

[b]UPDATE: H+96 hours
POV: Sergeant Kael Moret, 3rd Paratrooper Division[/b]

The ridge was ours, but holding it meant nothing if we couldnt bring in proper supply. High Command ordered us to begin construction on an improvised airstrip.

It was rough work. We leveled a long stretch of earth using whatever gear we could salvage. The engineers brought down portable ground-flatteners, but it was pickaxes and sweat that did most of the job. Drones mapped the ground while we dug, poured, packed, and reinforced.

We were three days in when the first sign came. A scout drone dropped from the sky with no warningjammed, EMPd, we didnt know. I ordered full alert.

Twenty minutes later, the ridge erupted.

Sal-Baliz came in wavesinfantry, mortars, makeshift artillery, and even a few captured recon drones. The whole western slope lit up with fire. We had less than thirty seconds warning.

The next 28 hours were blood and grit. Our foxholes turned into graves, rebuilt into trenches, and dug again. Our auto-turrets burned out by hour ten. Ammo was airlifted in by gunship, dropped under fire. At one point, they breached the northern flankwe took it back in hand-to-hand.

Corporal Jasso died holding the generator. Private Dorn, leg braced and still bleeding, manned a heavy machine gun and didnt let go until the barrel overheated.

And still, we held.

At the 28th hour, they broke.

We stood on the ridge, covered in dirt and ash, watching the last of them retreat through the smoke. Cheers were quietmost were too tired to celebrate. But when the radio crackled with the words, Landing gear inbound, we knew wed won.

The first supply bird touched down thirty minutes later on a half-finished strip soaked in blood.

[nation]Sal-Baliz[/nation] [nation]United Hydronia[/nation]

[b]There is no escape[/b]
In the dead of night, a team of soldiers were doing their routine tasks, at one the border outposts. Suddenly, a young man spotted something. As the searchlight swept through the empty desert, a reflective surface could be seen. After further investigation, the team found a young woman attempting to escape Sal-Baliz territory. The high command would not stand for this. The next day, the woman was brutally interrogated, to find out her home village. After being beaten, set on fire and even having limbs removed, she gave in and told them the location of Al-Sharwa. It turned out that this small village actually housed a Christian minority. A small army of 100 soldiers was sent to remove this village. All of its residents, Christian or not, were rounded up and one by one beheaded in front of the rest of the residents. The high command then proceeded to order the conversion of the village into a military settlement. SummitONE has been allowed full access to the village to do with it as they please.
